It has been needed four times in twenty years, and each time the member had already left the club,
which is a comfort of a kind and not much of one, and the letters are kept in the box with the rest.

The treasurer's handover happens at the annual general meeting and is a meeting of its own, with
the outgoing and incoming treasurers, the chair and the examiner, the deed box opened and its
contents listed, the bank mandate changed on the day, and these notes read through together. It
takes an afternoon and has never been regretted.

Questions from members about the money are answered by the treasurer, in person where
possible, and are welcome even when they are awkward, because a member who asks is a member
who has read the accounts. A question the treasurer cannot answer on the spot is answered in
writing within the week, and a question that turns out to have found a mistake is thanked for in the
next report by name if the member agrees. The club has had three treasurers who took questions
badly and none of them lasted, which is the lesson.

The launch and the trailer are the two things the club owns that can hurt somebody on a public
road or a public waterway, and both are insured, inspected and driven only by the members named
on the list by the boathouse door. The launch's fuel is bought on the club card by the captain and
logged against the engine hours; the trailer's tyres and lights are checked before every away regatta
by whoever is towing, and the check is signed for on the trailer sheet. Neither is lent to another club
without the committee's agreement.

Lastly, these notes are revised at each handover by the outgoing treasurer, with the incoming one,
and each version is dated and kept in the deed box. Most of the rules here were paid for by a lost
receipt, a surprised examiner or a boat that was insured for a year after it was sold, and the notes
are shorter than that list.

provenance.key:
has an owner, and the owner is the person the treasurer asks when the line goes over, which
happens, and is not a disgrace if it is explained at the meeting and minuted there.

Spending against the budget is reported at every meeting as a simple pair of columns, budget and
actual, with the difference and a word where the difference is more than a tenth. Members of the
committee are asked to read the sheet before the meeting; the ones who do ask better questions,
and the treasurer's job is easier for it, and shorter.

The club has no debts and borrows nothing, by long habit rather than by rule, and a proposal to
borrow for a boat or a building would need a general meeting and would get a long discussion. The
habit has kept the club through two recessions and a flood, and the treasurer who breaks it should
be sure of the reason and ready to explain it more than once, to the members, in writing.

Charity status was looked at in 2011 and declined, because the obligations outweighed the benefit
for a club of this size, and the papers from that decision are in the deed box for the next committee
that wonders. Gift Aid is available without it, through the community amateur sports club scheme,
and that is what the club uses, and has used since then.

The accounts, the budget, the reserve policy and these notes are on the shared drive where any
member can read them, and any member who asks the treasurer a question about them is
answered within the week, in writing if the question was in writing. A club whose money is visible
is a club whose treasurer is trusted, and the trust is worth the time.

The bar licence is held by the club and named to the chair, is renewed every year in September
through the council, and its conditions -- hours, the age rule, the sign by the door -- are the
committee's to enforce and the bar rota's to follow. A breach is the committee's problem before it is
the council's, and the committee has once had to close the bar for a month to make that point to a
rota that had stopped taking it seriously. The licence and the council's letters live in the deed box
with the lease.
